questions.text: Where is the bone pain located, how long have you had it, and is it constant or does it come and go?
questions.purpose: Characterise location, duration, and pattern; constant, worsening bone pain particularly at night suggests malignant aetiology
options: Localised to one site, less than 4 weeks, intermittent
Localised to one site, less than 4 weeks, constant
Localised to one site, more than 4 weeks, constant or worsening

questions.text: Is the bone pain worse at night or at rest, rather than during activity?
questions.purpose: Night pain and rest pain are red flags for malignant bone involvement, distinguishing it from mechanical musculoskeletal pain

questions.text: Do you have a known history of cancer (e.g. breast, prostate, lung, kidney, thyroid)?
questions.purpose: Prior cancer history significantly raises suspicion for bony metastases

questions.text: Have you experienced any weakness, numbness, or loss of bladder or bowel control alongside the back or spinal pain?
questions.purpose: Neurological signs with spinal pain suggest metastatic spinal cord compression — a surgical emergency

questions.text: Have you had any unexplained fractures or bone injuries after minimal or no trauma?
questions.purpose: Pathological fractures through tumour-involved bone are red flags for primary or metastatic bone malignancy

questions.text: Have you had unexplained weight loss, night sweats, or persistent fatigue alongside the bone pain?
questions.purpose: Constitutional B-symptoms with bone pain raise malignancy suspicion — particularly multiple myeloma or lymphoma

questions.text: Is there a visible or palpable swelling, lump, or bony prominence at the site of pain?
questions.purpose: A local mass at the pain site may indicate a primary bone tumour
